psr-j0835m4510.name: Vela Pulsar
psr-j0835m4510.introduction: is the spinning core of a star that exploded 11,000–12,300 years ago, about 900 light-years away in Vela. It turns 11 times a second and is the brightest pulsar in the radio sky and the brightest steady object in high-energy gamma rays. It is also known as PSR B0833-45 and PSR J0835-4510.

sections.title: Proof that supernovae make neutron stars
sections.text: In 1968, astronomers at the University of Sydney linked the pulsar to the Vela supernova remnant, the expanding debris of the explosion. It was direct evidence that a supernova leaves a neutron star behind. The remnant still expands at about 1,200 km/s, and the pulsar’s wind of particles lights a nebula of its own, Vela X.

sections.title: A clock that skips
sections.text: Vela is the best-known glitching pulsar. Every three years or so its steadily slowing spin suddenly speeds up, and no one can yet predict when. On 12 December 2016, a glitch was caught live, pulse by pulse, by the 26 m dish of the Mount Pleasant Radio Observatory. A glitch on 22 July 2021 shortened its period by about one part in a million.

sections.title: A signpost for aliens
sections.text: Vela is one of the 14 pulsars on the map engraved on the plaques of Pioneer 10 and 11, launched in 1972 and 1973, and repeated on the Voyager Golden Records. Each line’s length gives a pulsar’s distance from the Sun, and binary marks along it give its period. Because pulsars slow down, those periods even reveal when the probes left Earth.

sections.title: Pulses turned into music
sections.text: French composer Gérard Grisey turned the signals of Vela and PSR B0329+54 into sound for his 1989–90 work Le noir de l’étoile.

psr-j0633p1746.name: Geminga
psr-j0633p1746.introduction: is a neutron star in Gemini, roughly 600–800 light-years away, that was discovered as a puzzling source of gamma rays. It is the core of a star that exploded about 300,000 years ago and one of the nearest pulsars to the Sun. It is also known as PSR B0633+17 and PSR J0633+1746.

sections.title: “It’s not there”
sections.text: Giovanni Bignami built the name from “Gemini gamma-ray source” and the Milanese phrase gh’è minga, “it’s not there”: for years, nothing visible could be found at the gamma-ray position. The International Astronomical Union approved the name on 4 April 2022.

sections.title: Found before it was seen
sections.text: NASA’s SAS-2 satellite first recorded an excess of gamma rays here. The Einstein X-ray satellite later picked out a faint X-ray source, and in March 1991 ROSAT found it pulsing every 0.237 seconds, tying the X-rays to the gamma rays. In visible light Geminga is a magnitude 25.5 speck.

sections.title: A halo of antimatter
sections.text: In 2019, a Fermi telescope study revealed a large gamma-ray halo around Geminga, made by particles streaming away from it. Those particles might supply up to 20% of the high-energy positrons, the antimatter twins of electrons, measured by the AMS-02 experiment on the International Space Station.

sections.title: Racing across the sky
sections.text: Geminga crosses the sky at 0.178 arcseconds per year. At 250 parsecs, that is about 211 km/s, fast enough to travel from the Earth to the Moon in half an hour.

psr-j1921p2153.name: PSR B1919+21
psr-j1921p2153.introduction: is the first pulsar ever discovered, found in 1967 in Vulpecula. Its sharp radio pulse repeats every 1.337 seconds, and its distance is still uncertain, roughly 1,000–2,600 light-years. It is also known as CP 1919 and PSR J1921+2153.

sections.title: Little green men
sections.text: Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the signal on 28 November 1967 while working with her PhD supervisor Antony Hewish at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in Cambridge. The pulses were so regular that the team jokingly labeled the source LGM-1, for “little green men”. Its first catalog name, CP 1919, stands for Cambridge Pulsar at 19h 19m.

sections.title: A Nobel Prize without her
sections.text: The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hewish and Martin Ryle. Fred Hoyle argued that Bell Burnell should have shared it. In 2018 she received the $3 million Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics.

sections.title: An album cover
sections.text: A plot of its successive radio pulses, drawn by radio astronomer Harold Craft, became the cover of Joy Division’s 1979 debut album, Unknown Pleasures.

psr-j1300p1240.name: Lich
psr-j1300p1240.introduction: is a millisecond pulsar about 2,300 light-years away in Virgo, and the host of the first planets ever confirmed beyond the Solar System. It spins about 161 times a second. It is also known as PSR B1257+12 and PSR J1300+1240.

sections.title: The first exoplanets
sections.text: Aleksander Wolszczan discovered the pulsar with the Arecibo radio telescope on 9 February 1990. In 1992, he and Dale Frail showed that tiny, regular shifts in its pulses came from two orbiting planets; a third followed in 1994. They were the first extrasolar planets found, and the first known to orbit a pulsar.

sections.title: Three undead worlds
sections.text: In the IAU’s 2015 NameExoWorlds contest, the pulsar became Lich, an undead creature that controls other undead by magic. Its planets became Draugr (b), Poltergeist (c) and Phobetor (d). They orbit every 25, 67 and 98 days. Draugr has about 0.02 Earth masses, the lowest-mass planet found by any technique; the other two have about four Earth masses each.

sections.title: Planets that were not there
sections.text: A 1996 claim of a fourth, Saturn-like body was retracted. So was a later dwarf-planet idea: the timing oddities are not periodic and are fully explained by slow changes in the gas between the pulsar and Earth.

psr-j0437m4715-system.name: PSR J0437-4715
psr-j0437m4715-system.introduction: is the nearest and brightest millisecond pulsar known, about 510 light-years away in Pictor. The pulsar, A, spins about 174 times a second, and a cool helium white dwarf, B, circles it every 5.74 days.

sections.title: Steadier than an atomic clock
sections.text: The pulses of A keep time to about one part in 10¹⁵, arguably steadier than human-made atomic clocks. Until the Gaia mission, it was the most precisely located object outside the Solar System. It was also the first millisecond pulsar whose X-rays were studied in detail.

sections.title: Weighing a neutron star
sections.text: Timing by the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array weighs A at 1.418 ± 0.044 solar masses and B at 0.221. The same data fix the distance at 156.96 parsecs, uncertain by less than 0.1%, and tilt the orbit 137.5° to our line of sight. Those numbers anchor X-ray measurements of how large a neutron star is.

sections.title: A cool companion, a hot core
sections.text: Spectra show that B’s surface is only about 3,950 K, cooler than the Sun. Ultraviolet light from A tells the opposite story: its surface is between 125,000 and 350,000 K, a sign that something keeps heating the neutron star throughout its life.

psr-j1856m3754.name: RX J1856.5-3754
psr-j1856m3754.introduction: is a lone neutron star in Corona Australis, about 400 light-years away and one of the nearest known. It sends out no radio pulses; it was found in 1992 by its X-rays, from a surface at roughly 500,000 K. It is also known as PSR J1856-3754.

sections.title: One of the Magnificent Seven
sections.text: It belongs to the “Magnificent Seven”, a group of young, isolated neutron stars 130–500 parsecs from Earth.

sections.title: Younger than its spin suggests
sections.text: Its slowing spin makes it look about 3.8 million years old, but tracing its path back through the Galaxy tells a different story. It leads to the Upper Scorpius association, where the star was probably born about 420,000 years ago. Today it crosses the sky at about 190 km/s.

sections.title: Not a quark star after all
sections.text: Early estimates gave it a diameter of only 4–8 km, small enough to suggest a quark star, made of free quarks rather than neutrons. Later Chandra and Hubble data pushed the distance out and removed it from the quark-star candidates. Its radius is now put at about 12 km.

sections.title: Light bent by empty space
sections.text: In 2016, astronomers using ESO’s Very Large Telescope found its visible light to be about 16% polarized. That is evidence, though not proof, of vacuum birefringence: a quantum effect in which an extreme magnetic field makes empty space itself change the light passing through it.

sections.title: A pulse almost too faint to find
sections.text: Searches for a pulse came up empty for years. In 2007, XMM-Newton data finally showed one: the star turns once every 7.055 seconds, and its X-rays rise and fall by only about 1.2%, the weakest pulsing then seen from a lone X-ray pulsar. So it is both at once: a neutron star, and a pulsar that stays silent in radio.

psr-j1719m1438.name: PSR J1719-1438
psr-j1719m1438.introduction: is a millisecond pulsar in Serpens, circled every 2 hours and 11 minutes by a Jupiter-mass companion that may be made largely of carbon, nicknamed the “diamond planet”. Its distance is uncertain: electron-density models place it between about 1,100 and 3,900 light-years.

sections.title: A planet heavier than lead
sections.text: The companion has about the mass of Jupiter but at most 40% of its width, giving it a density of at least 23 g/cm³, twice that of lead. It is probably what remains of a white dwarf that the pulsar stripped down to a carbon and oxygen core.

sections.title: Closer than the Sun’s surface
sections.text: The High Time Resolution Survey found the pulsar in 2011, and timing with the Parkes and Lovell telescopes revealed the companion. It orbits only about 600,000 km away, less than the Sun’s radius: placed at the Sun’s center, its orbit would lie inside the Sun.

psr-j1614m2230-system.name: PSR J1614-2230
psr-j1614m2230-system.introduction: is a millisecond pulsar in Scorpius whose mass, nearly twice the Sun’s, overturned theories of what neutron stars are made of. The pulsar, A, spins about 317 times a second, and a white dwarf, B, orbits it every 8.7 days.

sections.title: Weighed by a delay
sections.text: Found in 2006 by the Parkes telescope, A was timed in 2010 with the Green Bank Telescope by Paul Demorest and colleagues. They measured how much B’s gravity delays the pulses passing it, the Shapiro delay, and found about 1.97 solar masses, the most massive neutron star then known.

sections.title: Too heavy for exotic matter
sections.text: A neutron star this heavy rules out models whose cores contain hyperons or kaon condensates: such stars would collapse into black holes before reaching this mass. Later timing revised the mass to about 1.9 solar masses.

psr-j2222m0137-system.name: PSR J2222-0137
psr-j2222m0137-system.introduction: is a pulsar about 880 light-years away in Aquarius, circled every 2.4 days by one of the coldest white dwarfs known. The pulsar, A, spins about 30 times a second; its companion, B, has never been seen.

sections.title: Too cold to see
sections.text: Even deep optical images show no trace of B. If it is a white dwarf, its surface must be colder than about 3,000 K, about half as hot as the Sun’s, which makes it among the coolest white dwarfs ever observed. To be so cold it must be very old, with an interior that has already crystallized.

sections.title: Two heavyweights
sections.text: Precise radio timing weighs A at 1.831 solar masses and B at 1.319. Together the two dead stars hold more than three times the mass of the Sun.

psr-j0659p1414.name: Monogem Pulsar
psr-j0659p1414.introduction: is a 110,000-year-old pulsar about 930 light-years away in Gemini, sitting inside the Monogem Ring, a large supernova remnant that glows in X-rays. It spins about 2.6 times a second and is also known as PSR B0656+14.

sections.title: A ring seen only in X-rays
sections.text: The Monogem Ring was found in the early 1970s by its soft X-rays. It shows no radio glow, because the gas it expands into is unusually thin, and models put its age at 68,000–100,000 years.

sections.title: Parent or passer-by?
sections.text: The pulsar, found in 1989, lies slightly off the ring’s center, and its motion points toward the center rather than away, which makes the link look unlikely. Yet its parallax distance of about 290 parsecs and its age both fit, so it may be the remnant’s own neutron star. The HAWC observatory has detected a halo of very-high-energy gamma rays around it.

psr-j2225p6535.name: Guitar Pulsar
psr-j2225p6535.introduction: is one of the fastest-moving pulsars known, about 2,900 light-years away in Cepheus. As it plows through interstellar gas, it pushes ahead a glowing bow shock, the Guitar Nebula. It is also known as PSR B2224+65.

sections.title: Faster than a million km per hour
sections.text: For a distance of 1–2 kiloparsecs, the pulsar travels at about 800–1,600 km/s, on the extreme tail of pulsar speeds.

sections.title: A guitar that changes shape
sections.text: Hubble imaged the nebula in the red light of hydrogen twice, seven years apart, and its outline had changed. The pulsar’s wind stayed steady, so the changes come from denser and thinner patches of gas that the pulsar runs into.

psr-j0453p1559-system.name: PSR J0453+1559
psr-j0453p1559-system.introduction: is a pair of dead stars about 1,700 light-years away in Taurus that orbit each other every 4.07 days. The pulsar, A, spins about 22 times a second; its partner, B, is silent and may be the lightest neutron star ever weighed.

sections.title: The most lopsided pair
sections.text: Every double neutron star known before had two nearly equal masses. Here A has 1.559 solar masses and B only 1.174, a ratio of 0.75. The masses come from the orbit’s slowly turning ellipse and from the delay of pulses passing B. If B is a neutron star, it is the lightest one measured precisely.

sections.title: A white dwarf in disguise?
sections.text: Supernova models struggle to make so light a neutron star. In 2019, Thomas Tauris and Hans-Thomas Janka proposed that B may instead be a white dwarf, left by a rare thermonuclear electron-capture supernova in a stripped star.

psr-j0357p3205.name: Morla
psr-j0357p3205.introduction: is a middle-aged pulsar in Perseus that pulses in gamma rays but not in radio, and drags a 9-arcminute tail of X-rays behind it. Its distance is estimated at 300–900 parsecs. It is also known as PSR J0357+3205.

sections.title: The fastest pulsar?
sections.text: If the tail glows the way its discoverers modeled it, Morla must race through space at about 1,900 km/s, faster than any other known pulsar. Its X-rays also make it the coldest neutron star known for its age.

gaia-bh1-system.name: Gaia BH1
gaia-bh1-system.introduction: is the nearest known black hole, about 1,560 light-years away in Ophiuchus, circled by a Sun-like star. The black hole, A, has about 9.3 solar masses; the star, B, is a G dwarf of 0.93 solar masses. The star is also known as Gaia DR3 4373465352415301632.

sections.title: Found by a wobble
sections.text: Gaia BH1 was found in 2022 from the motion of its star alone: Gaia’s position measurements and radial velocities showed the star circling something massive and invisible. The team led by El-Badry found no explanation other than a black hole, and a second team led by Chakrabarti detected it independently.

sections.title: An almost Earth-sized orbit
sections.text: The star and the black hole circle each other every 185.4 days at an average distance of 1.40 AU, a little farther than Earth is from the Sun. The orbit is noticeably stretched, with an eccentricity of 0.43. The black hole’s event horizon has a radius of only about 28 km.

gaia-bh3-system.name: Gaia BH3
gaia-bh3-system.introduction: is the most massive known stellar black hole in the Milky Way, about 1,930 light-years away in Aquila. The black hole, A, has about 33 solar masses; its companion, B, is an ancient, metal-poor giant star.

sections.title: Spotted ahead of schedule
sections.text: Astronomers found the system while checking Gaia measurements being prepared for the mission’s fourth data release, and announced it early, on 16 April 2024. It is the second known stellar black hole above roughly 10 solar masses, after Cygnus X-1.

sections.title: A stretched, 11-year orbit
sections.text: The pair circles every 11.6 years on an elongated orbit with an eccentricity of 0.73. Their separation swings between 4.5 and 29 AU, roughly the span from Jupiter’s orbit to Neptune’s.

sections.title: A relic of the young Galaxy
sections.text: The star has only about 1/360 of the Sun’s share of iron and belongs to ED-2, the stream of a disrupted star cluster in the Milky Way’s halo. The system probably formed more than 13 billion years ago.

sections.title: A cousin of the gravitational-wave black holes
sections.text: Its mass matches those of the merging black holes detected through gravitational waves. Its metal-poor companion supports the idea that such heavy black holes formed from metal-poor stars.

gaia-ns1-system.name: Gaia NS1
gaia-ns1-system.introduction: is an old, Sun-like star about 2,400 light-years away in Libra, circled every 731 days by an unseen companion of 1.9 solar masses that is most likely a neutron star. The unseen companion is A; the star is B, also known as Gaia DR3 6328149636482597888.

sections.title: Still a candidate
sections.text: Gaia’s astrometry and follow-up radial velocities weigh the unseen companion at 1.90 ± 0.04 solar masses, on a 2-year orbit tilted 68.7° to our view. A neutron star is the most likely explanation; a close pair of white dwarfs is disfavored but not fully ruled out.

sections.title: An ancient, lithium-rich star
sections.text: The star is a visitor from the Galactic halo near the end of its main-sequence life, at least 12 billion years old. It has about 1/17 of the Sun’s share of iron and an unusually high amount of lithium.

gaia-bh2-system.name: Gaia BH2
gaia-bh2-system.introduction: is a black hole about 3,800 light-years away in Centaurus, the third nearest known. It has about 8.9 times the Sun’s mass and gives itself away only by the pull it exerts on a red giant, which takes 1,277 days to circle it.

sections.title: An orbit too wide to explain
sections.text: When it was reported in 2023, its orbit was much longer than that of any black-hole binary studied before. It also seems too wide to have formed the textbook way, with the two stars sharing a common envelope of gas. The black hole barely feeds, which fits models in which little of the gas it could capture ever reaches it.

a0620-00-system.name: A0620-00
a0620-00-system.introduction: is a black hole about 4,700 light-years away in Monoceros, with a K-type star circling it every 7.75 hours. In 1975 it flared into the brightest X-ray point source in the sky; it had already erupted once, in 1917.

sections.title: A mass revised downward
sections.text: Its mass depends on how steeply the orbit tilts toward us. One careful study found a tilt of 51.0° and 6.6 solar masses. A 2017 revisit of the same kind of light curves found 54.1° and 5.86 solar masses, and warned that hidden errors may still exceed the quoted uncertainty.

ogle-2011-blg-0462.name: OGLE-2011-BLG-0462
ogle-2011-blg-0462.introduction: is a lone black hole about 5,000 light-years away in Sagittarius, the first isolated black hole ever confirmed. It has no companion to give it away; it was found in 2011 because its gravity bent the light of a star far behind it.

sections.title: Eleven years with Hubble
sections.text: Hubble tracked the tiny shift of that background star for 11 years. The latest analysis gives a mass of 7.15 ± 0.83 solar masses and finds no light from the object itself, which settles that it is a black hole. It moves at about 51 km/s relative to the stars around it.

xte-j1118p480-system.name: XTE J1118+480
xte-j1118p480-system.introduction: is a black hole about 5,500 light-years away in Ursa Major, circled by a small, cool star about every 4 hours. It has between 6.9 and 8.2 times the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: Far from the crowd
sections.text: Nearly all known black-hole X-ray transients lie in the Milky Way’s bulge and disk. This is one of only two at high Galactic latitude: seen from Earth, it sits 62° from the plane of the Galaxy.

cygnus-x-1-system.name: Cygnus X-1
cygnus-x-1-system.introduction: is a black hole about 7,200 light-years away in Cygnus, circled every 5.6 days by a supergiant star. Discovered on a rocket flight in 1964, it was the first X-ray source widely accepted to be a black hole, and it is still one of the strongest in the sky.

sections.title: Heavier than anyone expected
sections.text: A new radio parallax in 2021 moved it farther away than thought, and that raised its mass to 21.2 ± 2.2 solar masses. Finding so heavy a black hole in a metal-rich system puts a firm limit on how much mass massive stars can lose to their winds.

v404-cygni-system.name: V404 Cygni
v404-cygni-system.introduction: is a black hole of about 9 solar masses, roughly 7,800 light-years away in Cygnus. A giant star circles it every 6.47 days and feeds it, setting off outbursts first noted as a nova in 1938.

sections.title: A third star changes the story
sections.text: In 2024 astronomers found a third star at least 3,500 astronomical units away, still bound to the pair. Had the black hole been kicked hard at birth, that star would have been lost. Its kick must have been under about 5 km/s, so at least some black holes form with almost no kick at all.

sections.title: The first black hole with a parallax
sections.text: In 2009 radio astronomers measured its distance directly from its yearly shift against distant sources, 2.39 ± 0.14 kiloparsecs. It was the first accurate parallax distance to a black hole, and it came out significantly closer than the accepted value.

gro-j0422p32-system.name: GRO J0422+32
gro-j0422p32-system.introduction: is a black hole about 8,100 light-years away in Perseus, with a small red star circling it about every 5 hours. At roughly 2.7 solar masses it may be among the lightest black holes known.

sections.title: Inside the mass gap
sections.text: Few compact objects are known between the heaviest neutron stars and the lightest black holes. A 2022 study measured the orbit’s tilt from the shape of the gas disk’s glow, which put this one at 2.7 solar masses, inside that gap. It suggests the gap may largely reflect how few of these systems have been measured. An older estimate gave 3.97 solar masses.

gs-2000p25-system.name: GS 2000+25
gs-2000p25-system.introduction: is a black hole about 8,800 light-years away in Vulpecula, circled by a K-type star every 8.26 hours. It is the faintest quiescent black-hole X-ray binary yet measured.

sections.title: Almost perfectly quiet
sections.text: Deep Chandra observations caught it at about a billionth of the maximum brightness a black hole of its mass can sustain, the lowest X-ray luminosity seen in such a system. Fifteen hours with the Very Large Array found no radio emission at all.

maxi-j1820p070-system.name: MAXI J1820+070
maxi-j1820p070-system.introduction: is a black hole about 9,700 light-years away in Ophiuchus, circled by a small star every 16.5 hours. If the orbit shares the tilt of its radio jets, the black hole has about 8.5 solar masses.

sections.title: Jets at nearly light speed
sections.text: Its parallax of 0.348 ± 0.033 milliarcseconds gives a distance of 2.96 ± 0.33 kiloparsecs, with no model involved. That also pins down its jets, moving at about 0.89 times the speed of light, and shows its outburst peaked at only 15% of the theoretical limit.

xmmu-j173203.name: XMMU J173203.3-344518
xmmu-j173203.introduction: is a neutron star about 8,000 light-years away in Scorpius, at the centre of the supernova remnant HESS J1731-347. Models of its X-rays give it only about 0.77 solar masses, which would make it the lightest neutron star known.

sections.title: Too light for a neutron star?
sections.text: That is about half the mass of a typical neutron star, and less than standard theory predicts a supernova can leave behind. Its discoverers call it a promising candidate for a star of strange quark matter, though its properties still fit an ordinary neutron star. The mass comes from a model of its spectrum, not from weighing.

cxou-j085201.name: CXOU J085201.4-461753
cxou-j085201.introduction: is a neutron star at the centre of the supernova remnant Vela Jr, in Vela. Its distance is uncertain: estimates run from about 650 to 3,000 light-years, and no pulses have ever been seen.

sections.title: Listening for gravitational waves
sections.text: A spinning neutron star that is not perfectly round should hum in gravitational waves. Thousands of volunteers lent their computers to Einstein@Home to search LIGO data for this star’s signal, testing more than 10¹⁸ possible waveforms. None was found, which limits how lopsided the star can be.

rx-j1605.name: RX J1605.3+3249
rx-j1605.introduction: is a lone neutron star about 1,300 light-years away in Corona Borealis, one of the “Magnificent Seven” that shine softly in X-rays as they cool. Its distance is estimated from how much gas absorbs its light.

sections.title: The one that will not show its spin
sections.text: It is the only one of the seven whose rotation is still unconfirmed. An early 6.9-second signal did not hold up in later observations, and a 3.39-second candidate has yet to be confirmed.

psr-j0420m5022.name: RX J0420.0-5022
psr-j0420m5022.introduction: is a lone neutron star about 1,100 light-years away in Dorado, one of the “Magnificent Seven”. It is the coolest of the group, and at one turn every 3.45 seconds it has the fastest confirmed spin of the seven.

sections.title: Measured by the gas in the way
sections.text: No parallax exists for it. Its distance comes from how much interstellar gas dims its X-rays, compared with a three-dimensional map of the gas around the Sun.

psr-j0806m4123.name: RX J0806.4-4123
psr-j0806m4123.introduction: is a lone neutron star about 780 light-years away in Puppis, one of the “Magnificent Seven”. It turns once every 11.37 seconds, the slowest spin of the group.

sections.title: Dimmed by local gas
sections.text: Its distance, about 240 parsecs, comes from comparing the gas that absorbs its X-rays with maps of sodium gas around the Sun. The method is good to about 25 parsecs here, close to the edge of those maps.

psr-j1809m1943.name: XTE J1810-197
psr-j1809m1943.introduction: is a magnetar about 8,200 light-years away in Sagittarius, a neutron star with an enormous magnetic field that turns every 5.54 seconds. It is the first magnetar with a measured parallax.

sections.title: A magnetar pinned down
sections.text: Radio observations from 2019 and 2020, combined with two from 2006, gave a parallax of 0.40 ± 0.05 milliarcseconds. That places it about 2.5 kiloparsecs away, closer than earlier estimates. Its speed across the sky, about 200 km/s, turned out to be ordinary for a pulsar.

psr-j0418p5732.name: SGR 0418+5729
psr-j0418p5732.introduction: is a magnetar in Camelopardalis that turns once every 9.08 seconds. Its distance is not measured; astronomers usually assume about 6,500 light-years.

sections.title: Nothing to see in visible light
sections.text: Hubble imaged the field in 2011 and found no counterpart in visible or near-infrared light at the star’s position, which sets a strict limit on anything bright around it.

scorpius-x-1-system.name: Scorpius X-1
scorpius-x-1-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 7,600 light-years away in Scorpius, pulling gas from a low-mass companion that orbits every 18.9 hours. Found in 1962, it was the first X-ray source discovered beyond the Solar System and, apart from the Sun, it is the strongest steady X-ray source in the sky.

sections.title: Unmasking the companion
sections.text: The companion is lost in the glare of the hot gas around the neutron star. In 2002 astronomers finally caught its motion, using narrow emission lines from the side of the star lit by X-rays.

centaurus-x-4-system.name: Centaurus X-4
centaurus-x-4-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 6,200 light-years away in Centaurus, feeding from a K-type star that circles it every 15.1 hours. It flared in 1969 and 1979 and has not had a full outburst since.

sections.title: A spotted companion
sections.text: High-resolution spectra allowed astronomers to weigh the system and to map the companion’s surface, the first such map of a star in an X-ray binary. It turned out to be covered in starspots.

vela-x-1-system.name: Vela X-1
vela-x-1-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 6,600 light-years away in Vela, circling the blue supergiant HD 77581 every 8.964 days and turning once every 283 seconds. It is the textbook example of a neutron star feeding on a giant star’s wind.

sections.title: Eclipsed every orbit
sections.text: The neutron star disappears behind its companion for about two days of every orbit. The supergiant itself varies around magnitude 7, just too faint for the naked eye.

x-persei-system.name: X Persei
x-persei-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 2,000 light-years away in Perseus, orbiting a Be star every 250 days. It is an unusually slow pulsar, turning only once every 837 seconds, yet its X-rays are exceptionally energetic, reaching beyond 100 keV.

sections.title: Among the most magnetized
sections.text: Its magnetic field is not known precisely, but indirect signs put it above 10¹³ gauss. That would make it one of the most strongly magnetized X-ray pulsars known.

a0535p26-system.name: A0535+26
a0535p26-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 6,200 light-years away in Taurus, on a stretched 111-day orbit around the Be star HDE 245770. Each close pass can set off a burst of X-rays.

sections.title: A giant outburst in 2009
sections.text: In December 2009 it erupted to about 5 times the brightness of the Crab in hard X-rays. One orbit later came another, unexpectedly bright flare.

ls-i-61-303-system.name: LS I +61 303
ls-i-61-303-system.introduction: is a neutron star about 8,600 light-years away in Cassiopeia, on a 26.5-day orbit around a hot B-type star. It belongs to the rare gamma-ray binaries, which emit most of their power as gamma rays.

sections.title: Pulses at last
sections.text: For decades nobody could say what the compact object was. In 2020 China’s FAST radio telescope caught radio pulses every 269 milliseconds, the first pulses seen from it at any wavelength. They soon vanished again, but they strongly argue for a spinning neutron star.

psr-j0534p2200.name: Crab Pulsar
psr-j0534p2200.introduction: is the young neutron star at the heart of the Crab Nebula, about 6,200 light-years away in Taurus, left by the supernova seen from Earth in 1054. It spins about 30 times a second, and its wind powers most of the nebula’s glow.

sections.title: The pulsar that sealed the case
sections.text: Found in 1968, it was the first pulsar connected with a supernova remnant. It is also one of very few pulsars seen flashing in visible light, and it emits from radio waves up to gamma rays.

psr-j0737m3039a.name: PSR J0737-3039
psr-j0737m3039a.introduction: is the first known double pulsar: two neutron stars about 3,600 light-years away in Puppis, both seen as radio pulsars, circling each other every 2.45 hours. Found in 2003 at Parkes, it is known as A and B.

sections.title: A precision test of gravity
sections.text: Sixteen years of timing weighed the pair at 1.338185 and 1.248868 solar masses and made it one of the sharpest tests of general relativity for strong gravity. It also revealed relativistic effects never measured before.

psr-j1959p2048-system.name: Black Widow Pulsar
psr-j1959p2048-system.introduction: is a millisecond pulsar about 4,600 light-years away in Sagitta, spinning once every 1.6 milliseconds. Discovered in 1988, it was the first pulsar found to be destroying its companion.

sections.title: Eating its partner
sections.text: A tiny companion circles it every 9.2 hours and blocks the pulses for about 20 minutes per orbit. Winds of energetic particles from the pulsar are thought to be stripping it away, which inspired the name. Around 41 such “black widows” were known by 2023.

psr-j1939p2134.name: PSR B1937+21
psr-j1939p2134.introduction: is the first millisecond pulsar discovered, about 9,500 light-years away in Vulpecula. Found in 1982, it spins 642 times a second.

sections.title: A spin nobody expected
sections.text: Astronomers did not think pulsars could turn so fast. The discovery led to the idea that an old pulsar can be spun up by gas taken from a companion.

sections.title: Closer than it seemed
sections.text: A 2023 radio parallax places it at about 2.9 kiloparsecs, nearer than the 3.5 kiloparsecs adopted before.

psr-j0740p6620.name: PSR J0740+6620
psr-j0740p6620.introduction: is one of the most massive neutron stars with a precise mass, about 3,750 light-years away in Camelopardalis. It spins once every 2.9 milliseconds in orbit with a white dwarf.

sections.title: Near the limit
sections.text: Timing measures how its companion’s gravity delays the pulses, which gives a mass of 2.08 ± 0.07 solar masses. That is close to the theoretical maximum, so it strongly constrains what matter does at the highest densities.

psr-j0348p0432-system.name: PSR J0348+0432
psr-j0348p0432-system.introduction: is a pulsar about 6,800 light-years away in Taurus, in a tight orbit with a white dwarf. It was once counted among the heaviest neutron stars known.

sections.title: Two solar masses no more
sections.text: A 2013 study gave it 2.01 solar masses, relying on a model of the white dwarf’s light. Timing with the CHIME telescope gave 1.806 ± 0.037 in 2024, about 10% lower. For the first time for this pulsar, timing alone significantly constrains the mass.

psr-j0337p1715-system.name: PSR J0337+1715
psr-j0337p1715-system.introduction: is a millisecond pulsar about 4,200 light-years away in Taurus and the first found in a triple system. A white dwarf circles it closely, and a second one orbits both about every 11 months.

sections.title: Einstein’s falling test
sections.text: The outer star’s pull acts on both the dense pulsar and the light inner white dwarf. If gravity treated them differently, the timing would show it. In 2018 they were found to fall alike to better than a few parts per million, while the pulsar’s mass came out at 1.4359 solar masses.

psr-j0821m4300.name: PSR J0821-4300
psr-j0821m4300.introduction: is the “Cosmic Cannonball”, a fast-moving neutron star about 7,200 light-years away in Puppis, flung from the explosion that made the Puppis A supernova remnant.

sections.title: Thrown from its birthplace
sections.text: The remnant’s light first reached Earth about 3,700 years ago, and the star has been racing away from the blast ever since.

psr-j1537p1155-system.name: PSR J1537+1155
psr-j1537p1155-system.introduction: is a pair of neutron stars about 3,000 light-years away in Serpens, also known as PSR B1534+12. One is seen as a pulsar with a 37.9-millisecond spin.

sections.title: Two near-twins
sections.text: Twenty-two years of timing measured five relativistic effects in the orbit and weighed the pair at 1.3330 and 1.3455 solar masses, offering a clean test of gravity.
